 'I don't have friends. I never thought it was important': PRUE LEITH reveals her struggles with making companions, how it's one of the few regrets of her life... and her advice to Nigella Lawson about Paul Hollywood
 By JENNY JOHNSTON 
 Published: 06:49 EST, 14 November 2026 | Updated: 09:09 EST, 14 November 2026 
 --> 
 --> 
 --> Dame Prue Leith reckons she wrote seven books in the nine years she was a judge on The Great British Bake Off . 
 Seven! Mostly cookbooks but also a novel and a memoir, they were all written in the Winnebago she shared with Paul Hollywood while they were waiting for cakes to come out of the oven. ‘A showstopper can take four or five hours,’ she explains. What else would she be doing in that time?
 She stressed the extraordinary amount of downtime between filming segments as a great ‘boon’ to Nigella Lawson when handing over the baton for the role in September. I ask what Paul was doing while she was furiously scribbling. ‘Watching the racing,’ she says.
 Not that she’s accusing her former TV husband, as she thought of him, of being a slouch. She says he pretty much is Bake Off, and could judge the whole thing himself – but we will come to this. For now, she rather envies Paul’s ability to put his feet up. He’s spent years urging her to do the same, wondering why Prue, 86, feels the need to work endlessly when she could be on a sun lounger.
 ‘He’s always saying, “Why don’t you stop working and spend more time on the beach?” Paul goes to Cyprus a lot. As soon as Bake Off finishes [it’s filmed in the summer] he’s off, or he’s flying aeroplanes or driving fast cars. I really admire this. He doesn’t work just because he’s asked to. I tend to say yes to everything because I think, “Oh well, that’ll be interesting.” So I end up doing much more work than he does.
 ‘I’m a bit restless. I always want to do new things. He’s got a really admirable contentment with what he has. He’s very good at his job, and he’s really loyal to Bake Off.’ So what is wrong with you, Prue? ‘What is wrong with me?’ she says, laughing. ‘It all comes down to greed. I always want to do more.’
 The official line about why she quit the show is that she wanted to be able to have a summer holiday, and the filming schedule never allowed that. That is true. This summer she actually did have an extended break, travelling in Poland, Latvia and Estonia with her husband John for a month, then taking a house near Biarritz for the whole family. 
 It was a novelty, ‘so definitely worth giving up Bake Off’. But boredom, and the need for adventure, was a factor too.
 The official line about why Prue Leith quit Bake Off is that she wanted to be able to have a summer holiday, and the filming schedule never allowed that
 I’m reminded that her good friend Sandi Toksvig, who presented Bake Off from 2017 to 2020, bowed out of the show complaining her brain was ‘atrophying’ because there was so much ‘standing by, watching meringues dry’; and Prue had just been away with Sandi before announcing she was quitting Bake Off. 
 They’d travelled to Prue’s native South Africa to make a travel documentary, which begins on Channel 4 later this month. 
 Hot-air balloons had been involved! And naked men! Having watched the first episode of Prue & Sandi’s South African Adventure, I’m not surprised she came home and decided life was too short to wait for cakes to bake.
 The idea of Prue and Sandi, 68, doing some sort of travel show had been mooted years ago but it had never quite happened. They were away for a full month. Combined age 154. Combined intellect: formidable, although Prue is very modest here. ‘I’m not stupid and I’m always interested in learning, but Sandi was the walking encyclopaedia. She knew more than some of the tour guides.’
 There are some very serious parts to the series – not least Prue’s exploration of the guilt that comes with growing up as a white person with black nannies during apartheid, and recalling ‘venerable old black men stepping off the pavement to let us giggling schoolgirls past. I don’t think we even said thank you. I’m quite ashamed.’
 But there are parts of the show that are a hoot, the two women morphing into giggling teenagers. Their cable car trip up Table Mountain, for instance. One minute they’re admiring the rock layers, the next they’ve spied an unexpected formation.
 ‘Sandi got over-excited because there was a guy sunbathing naked on the cliff edge. Obviously he thought he was alone, he wasn’t reckoning on a cable car full of tourists. Sandi set up a waving friendship with this fellow. They were waving wildly to each other.’
 Prue is still laughing. What’s interesting is that every evening the pair chose to hang out together. ‘Often when you’re filming, all you want to do is slope off to your hotel, have room service and go to sleep, but we always had dinner together. Being with Sandi just brings me great joy.’
 Prue says of her former co-judge: ‘He’s a terrific baker. To watch him knead is magic'
 Prue with Sandi Toksvig on Prue & Sandi’s South African Adventure
 The show isn’t billed as a study of female friendship in later life, but that’s what it becomes. There’s another lovely moment when Sandi teases Prue about the fact they look like they’re starting a geriatric girl band. Who else would she have in her girl band, I ask her today. ‘Joanna Lumley, because I love her,’ she says. ‘Although we’d probably also need someone who could sing.’
 When we talk about real-life female friendship, though, an astonishing thing emerges. Although Sandi is a true friend, ‘one you could call at two in the morning and she’d be there for you’, when I ask who else is in Prue’s network of close female confidantes, she can’t think of a single name.
 ‘It’s Sandi. And now Debbie, her wife. I’ve been very bad at friendship,’ she admits, citing it as one of the only regrets she has in life. ‘I never thought it was important. If someone had said, “You don’t have any friends,” I’d have said, “What do we need friends for?” It didn’t occur to me it was unwise.’
 She wrote about this in her book Being Old… And Learning To Love It!, urging younger women to invest in friendships in a way she never did. It was partly because she was building an empire (before her TV career there were restaurants and a cookery school). There were also two children, Daniel and Li-Da.
 ‘I had a very happy first marriage, but when your husband is your best friend you tend to neglect all that. Rayne [Kruger, whom she married in 1974] was very reclusive too. 
 'He didn’t need friends, and I was perfectly happy with that. I was working in London in the week, coming home on a Thursday, and when I did I was quite happy to have scrambled eggs with the children. I didn’t want to see anyone else because I was tired from work. Later, I regretted that. When Rayne died I was bloody lonely. I didn’t have friends, didn’t even know my neighbours. It never occurred to me at the time.’
 Rayne was a family friend during her childhood, the husband of her mum’s best friend. He was a father-figure who became a mentor, a business partner and then lover. They had a clandestine affair for 13 years before he left his wife to marry Prue. Was this a factor in not forming friendships at the time most young women are forging lifelong ones?
 ‘It could have been,’ she says. ‘For 13 years our relationship was a secret so it would have restricted all that, but even after it we had more than 25 years of marriage, and we didn’t see the need for friends. I never ever went out with just a girlfriend. I didn’t have any. But when he died I thought, “Oops!” Not to even know my neighbours…’ her voice tails off. ‘I’m sure there are lots of people who could have been my friends.’
 The show isn’t billed as a study of female friendship in later life, but that’s what it becomes
 Sandi is a true friend, says Prue, ‘one you could call at two in the morning and she’d be there for you’
 Prue says she warned Nigella Lawson (with Paul Hollywood on Bake Off's latest series) that 'you have to hold your own because Paul could do this show without you'
 Prue was single for eight years after Rayne died in 2002, until she met John Playfair. She’s spoken before about how her now husband brought lots of things into her life – most famously colour. It was because of John, who’d worked in the fashion industry, that she started wearing the brightly hued glasses and necklaces that became her TV trademark.
 He also brought friends to the table of their Cotswolds home. ‘Unlike me, John is good at friendship. He knows everyone. He has all the friends, and he makes new ones all the time.’
 Since she married John, she says she’s ‘muscled in’ on his friends. ‘They’ve become our friends, so that if he pops his clogs I’ll still have friends.’ I’m not sure I’ve ever heard a high-profile woman talk so honestly about this. Most women would be reluctant to say ‘I don’t have friends’ out loud. 
 ‘That’s probably true, but I think most people do have friends,’ says Prue. ‘I think of my daughter and her age group. They’re always going out with a gang of girls. Maybe younger people are better at it.’
 It’s touching, and she clearly treasures Sandi. ‘You shouldn’t be friends with someone for this reason, but I know that if I needed something, she’d be there. I hope I’d do the same for her. It’s not just the selfish thing that you need someone to call when you fall down the stairs, it’s that friends bring pleasure and more to your life than is in your life, and Sandi does.’
 But didn’t Prue tell me once that Paul Hollywood had become a friend? Hadn’t he once landed his helicopter on her lawn, and come to dinner? ‘He’s a friend, but more the sort you see once a year. He’s great fun to have dinner with, but it’s a deeper friendship with Sandi. She and I have lots in common. Women’s rights, politics, books. I’m not interested in the things Paul’s interested in – cars, planes, anything with an engine.’
 There’s another illuminating confession regarding Paul. She really does believe he could do Bake Off on his own. ‘He’s a terrific baker. To watch him knead is magic. And he’s been part of the show from the start, so knows everything. He could easily judge Bake Off all by himself. 
 'I did say to Nigella, “You have to hold your own because Paul could do this show without you. You’re only there because the production company thinks they want two judges and one of them has to be a woman.” When I started I was slightly intimidated by him. My instinct was to say, “You are right,” or stand there like a nodding donkey, agreeing with everything he said.’
 It’s quite a stretch to imagine Prue as a nodding donkey, but she says that Nigella, as a keen baker, is already better qualified for the job than she was. ‘I’m not a champion baker. I’m just a damn good set of taste buds.’
 Prue & Sandi’s South African Adventure starts on Tuesday, November 24 on Channel 4.
